stem: A database administrator can query the customer table and read card numbers in full. Policy says only the payments application should ever see them. The server already uses full disk encryption. What addresses the requirement?

options.text: Record or column level encryption, so the field is only readable by holders of that key
options.why: The threat is an authorised database user, so protection must sit above the database's own access. Encrypting the column means the DBA sees ciphertext even on a successful query.

options.text: Full disk encryption, which is already protecting the data at rest
options.why: Disk encryption is transparent once the machine is running. Every query returns plaintext, which is why it does nothing against a legitimate user.

options.text: Transport encryption between the application and the database
options.why: That protects the wire. The DBA is reading the data at rest, not intercepting it.

options.text: Partition encryption on the volume holding the database files
options.why: Same blind spot as full disk: transparent to anything running on the booted system.

stem: A laptop is stolen from a parked car. It was powered off and used full disk encryption with the key sealed to the machine's TPM. What is the practical exposure?

options.text: Low: the disk is unreadable without the boot sequence succeeding and the user credential being supplied
options.why: This is the scenario full disk encryption is built for. The TPM only releases the key when boot measurements match, so moving the disk to another machine yields nothing.

options.text: High: the TPM stores the key in plaintext and can be read off the board
options.why: A TPM is designed to resist exactly that, and it will not release a sealed key when the boot state differs.

options.text: High: full disk encryption only protects files created after it was enabled
options.why: Enabling it encrypts the existing volume as well.

options.text: Low, but only because the data was also hashed at rest
options.why: Hashing is one way and would make the data unusable. Nothing in the scenario involves hashing.

stem: Two servers with no prior shared secret need to agree on a symmetric session key across an untrusted network, such that an observer recording the entire exchange cannot derive it. Which mechanism achieves this?

options.text: Diffie-Hellman key exchange
options.why: Each side contributes a secret and they derive the same shared value without it ever crossing the wire. This is the problem asymmetric key exchange was invented to solve.

options.text: Encrypting the symmetric key with AES and sending it
options.why: Circular: encrypting the key with a symmetric cipher requires a shared key you do not yet have.

options.text: Hashing the key with SHA-256 before transmission
options.why: Hashing is irreversible, so the recipient could never obtain the key. Hashing is not a transport mechanism.

options.text: Sending the key over the same channel with a longer key length
options.why: Length does not help when the observer receives the key itself.

stem: A colleague argues that a 2048-bit RSA key must be far stronger than a 256-bit AES key because the number is larger. What is the correct response?

options.text: Key lengths are only comparable within an algorithm family; 256-bit AES and 2048-bit RSA sit at broadly similar security levels
options.why: Symmetric and asymmetric keys resist different mathematics, so the bit counts are not on the same scale. This is why the numbers look so different for comparable strength.

options.text: They are correct; longer keys are always stronger regardless of algorithm
options.why: Comparing across families this way is exactly the error. A 2048-bit symmetric key would be absurd, not eight times better.

options.text: RSA is weaker because asymmetric algorithms are always weaker than symmetric ones
options.why: They solve different problems and are not ranked against each other. RSA is slower, not weaker.

options.text: Both are obsolete and only elliptic curve algorithms should be used
options.why: ECC achieves comparable strength with smaller keys, which is efficiency. AES-256 and RSA-2048 remain in standard use.

stem: An employee leaves abruptly and the organisation must read files they encrypted with a personal certificate. Which arrangement, if established beforehand, makes this possible?

options.text: Key escrow, in which a copy of the key is held by a trusted third party or the organisation itself
options.why: Escrow exists for precisely this: recoverability when the key holder is unavailable. The trade is that the escrowed copy is another place the key can be stolen from.

options.text: Key stretching applied to the user's passphrase
options.why: Stretching makes a weak passphrase expensive to brute force. It does not give anyone else access.

options.text: A longer key length on the user's certificate
options.why: That makes recovery harder, not easier.

options.text: Publishing the user's certificate to a public directory
options.why: A published certificate contains the public key. Decryption needs the private key, which is never published.

stem: An internal certificate authority's private signing key must be generated and used in hardware, never exported, with tamper evidence and certification suitable for audit. Which component fits?

options.text: A hardware security module
options.why: An HSM is a dedicated, certified, tamper-evident device for high-assurance key generation and operations, serving many systems. A CA signing key is its archetypal use.

options.text: The CA server's TPM
options.why: A TPM anchors trust for its own host and is soldered to one board. It is not built for the assurance level or the operational role of a CA key.

options.text: A secure enclave on the CA server's processor
options.why: Enclaves isolate operations from the host OS, chiefly on endpoints and mobile devices. They do not provide the certification and tamper evidence an audited CA requires.

options.text: A software key management system with the key stored encrypted on disk
options.why: A KMS manages lifecycle, often backed by an HSM. A key encrypted on disk can still be exported, which is the requirement being ruled out.

stem: A workstation refuses to release its disk encryption key after someone changes the boot order and attaches an external boot device. Which component enforced this?

options.text: The TPM, which only unseals the key when boot measurements match the expected state
options.why: Measured boot is the TPM's core function. Sealing a key to a boot state means tampering with that state makes the key unavailable rather than merely detectable.

options.text: The HSM attached to the workstation
options.why: Workstations do not carry HSMs; they are appliances serving many systems, used where the assurance justifies the cost.

options.text: The key management system refusing to issue the key
options.why: A KMS handles lifecycle and policy, not local boot measurement on an individual machine.

options.text: Key escrow policy blocking recovery
options.why: Escrow is about who else holds a copy, not about boot integrity.

stem: An administrator needs a publicly trusted certificate for a new web server. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Generate the key pair and CSR on the web server, send the CSR to the CA, install the returned certificate
options.why: The private key is generated where it will live and never travels. The CSR carries only the public key and the identity details to be vouched for.

options.text: Ask the CA to generate the key pair and email both halves to the administrator
options.why: A private key sent by email has been exposed to every system that handled the message. The key should never leave the host that will use it.

options.text: Generate a self-signed certificate first, then submit it to the CA for counter-signing
options.why: CAs sign certificate signing requests, not existing self-signed certificates.

options.text: Submit the private key in the CSR so the CA can verify key ownership
options.why: A CSR contains the public key and is self-signed to prove possession of the private key. The private key itself is never included.

stem: An organisation holds a wildcard certificate for *.example.com, deployed across eleven servers. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It covers one subdomain level only, and a compromise of the single private key affects every server using it
options.why: Both halves are the trade. *.example.com matches shop.example.com but not a.b.example.com, and spreading one private key across eleven hosts means eleven chances to lose it once.

options.text: It covers all subdomains at any depth beneath example.com
options.why: A wildcard matches a single label. Multi-level coverage needs additional names or separate certificates.

options.text: Each server receives its own distinct private key derived from the wildcard
options.why: They share the same certificate and the same private key, which is the concentration of risk.

options.text: It also covers example.com itself without a separate entry
options.why: The bare domain usually needs to be listed explicitly as a subject alternative name.

stem: An internal monitoring tool reachable only from the corporate LAN presents a self-signed certificate, and staff browsers show a warning. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Issue the certificate from the organisation's internal CA, whose root is already trusted by managed devices
options.why: An internal CA gives trust without a public certificate, and without training staff to click through warnings, which is the real damage of leaving it.

options.text: Instruct staff to accept the warning, since the service is internal
options.why: It teaches people to dismiss exactly the warning that matters elsewhere, and on an internal network an on-path attacker is still possible.

options.text: Buy a publicly trusted certificate from a third-party CA
options.why: Workable but unnecessary, and a public CA may not issue for an internal-only name.

options.text: Disable TLS on the service, since the warning is the only problem
options.why: That removes the encryption rather than fixing the trust, leaving credentials in the clear.

stem: An investigation finds that image files uploaded to a public gallery contained extracted customer records embedded in their pixel data. Which technique was used?

options.text: Steganography
options.why: Concealing a message inside another file so its existence is not apparent. It appears on the exam mostly in exfiltration scenarios, because it hides that anything is happening.

options.text: Tokenisation
options.why: Tokenisation replaces a value with a surrogate inside a system. It does not conceal data inside another file.

options.text: Data masking
options.why: Masking hides part of a value from a viewer. It is a presentation control, not a covert channel.

options.text: Asymmetric encryption
options.why: Encryption makes content unreadable but obvious. Steganography does the opposite: readable if found, but not apparent at all.

stem: Which of these techniques is, by design, the only one from which the original value cannot be recovered at all?

options.text: Hashing
options.why: A one-way function. Verification works by hashing the candidate and comparing, never by reversing. That is exactly why it suits password storage and integrity checking.

options.text: Tokenisation
options.why: The original is recoverable through the vault that holds the mapping. That recoverability is the feature.

options.text: Data masking
options.why: Depending on technique the underlying value often still exists and is simply not displayed.

options.text: Symmetric encryption
options.why: Reversible with the key, which is its entire purpose.

stem: Several competing firms want a shared record of transactions that any of them can verify, that none can quietly alter, and that needs no central authority. Which property does an open public ledger NOT provide?

options.text: Confidentiality of the recorded entries
options.why: Open means readable by all participants, which is what makes independent verification possible. Secrecy is the one thing it deliberately gives up.

options.text: Integrity of the recorded history
options.why: Each block commits to the previous one by hash, so altering an earlier entry invalidates everything after it.

options.text: Non-repudiation of individual entries
options.why: Entries are signed by the key that authorised them, which is what non-repudiation means.

options.text: Availability of the record to all participants
options.why: Replication across independent participants is how it survives any one of them going away.

stem: Credentials are being captured by an attacker sniffing traffic on a shared network segment between an application server and its database. Which control addresses this?

options.text: Transport encryption on the connection between the two systems
options.why: The exposure is on the wire, so the protection must be on the wire. Encryption at rest on either end does nothing for traffic in flight.

options.text: Full disk encryption on both servers
options.why: Protects the disks if the machines are stolen while off. Irrelevant to traffic between them.

options.text: File level encryption of the database files
options.why: Protects the stored files. The data is decrypted before it is sent, which is where it is being captured.

options.text: Hashing the credentials before transmission
options.why: A captured hash can often be replayed directly, and the receiving system still needs something it can verify against.

stem: Which TWO practices belong to sound key management rather than to algorithm choice? (Choose two.)

options.text: Defining rotation, revocation and destruction procedures for every key in use
options.why: Lifecycle management is the core of key management, and the part most often left undone until a key must be revoked in a hurry.

options.text: Holding escrowed copies of keys so encrypted business data remains recoverable
options.why: A deliberate availability trade-off, managed through policy and custody, not a property of any algorithm.

options.text: Selecting AES-256 over 3DES
options.why: That is algorithm selection. It matters, and it is a different decision from how the resulting keys are handled.

options.text: Choosing elliptic curve over RSA for smaller keys at equivalent strength
options.why: Also algorithm selection, concerned with efficiency rather than custody.

options.text: Using SHA-256 rather than MD5 for integrity checking
options.why: Primitive selection. No key is involved in a plain hash at all.

stem: A retailer must keep card numbers usable for refunds but wants them absent from the transaction database entirely, so that a database compromise yields nothing of value. Which approach fits?

options.text: Tokenisation, storing surrogates with the real values held in a separate vault
options.why: The real value is not in the database at all, which is stronger than encrypting it there, and the vault can still return it when a refund requires it.

options.text: Transparent database encryption of the whole database
options.why: Transparent means any authorised query returns plaintext. It protects the files, not the contents from a working session.

options.text: Hashing the card numbers before storage
options.why: Irreversible, so refunds become impossible. Card number space is also small enough to be brute forced from a hash.

options.text: Full disk encryption on the database server
options.why: Transparent once running, and the database still holds real card numbers.

stem: Why is it said that an entry written to a blockchain cannot be quietly altered later?

options.text: Each block includes a hash of the previous block, so changing an old entry changes every hash after it and the alteration is visible to everyone holding a copy
options.why: The property is tamper evidence, produced by chaining hashes and replicating the chain. It is detection by consensus, not a physical prohibition on editing bytes.

options.text: Entries are encrypted with a key that is destroyed after writing
options.why: A public ledger is readable by design. Destroying a key would also destroy access for the participants who need to verify it.

options.text: The storage medium is physically write-once
options.why: The chain runs on ordinary storage across ordinary machines. Nothing about the hardware prevents a write.

options.text: A central authority validates and locks each entry as it is written
options.why: Operating without a central authority is the defining characteristic. Validation comes from distributed consensus.
